talks.title: Why Mandatory Age Verification Keeps Us All Less Safe
talks.teaser: Argues that mandatory age verification laws weaken privacy and safety for everyone, and offers ways to push back on them.
talks.summary:
This EFF talk argues that mandatory age verification harms everyone, not only the people it targets. The speaker points to a vendor that promoted a verification library as a solved problem before it was embedded in any real app. A reviewer in the EU later found the zero-knowledge proof component still missing from the implementation. The lesson is that officials and the public should check what is actually built, since promises about protecting kids often fall apart in deployment.

The middle of the talk focuses on children. The speaker says bans can cut young people off from the people and resources that help them, including families and support services, and that exploited or isolated teens often need someone to tell. Blanket bans also leave kids unprepared when they gain access at 16, without media literacy or private-messaging skills. Engagement-driven features such as behavioral advertising and microtransactions are presented as the mechanisms worth regulating. Shared household devices raise further questions, and the speaker notes that a tool to tell which person is using a device would amount to a strong surveillance tool.

The closing section is practical. The speaker says age verification laws are not inevitable and cites the UK government's rollback of its digital identity scheme as evidence that pressure works. Listeners are urged to contact representatives, attend local hearings, organize, and oppose VPN bans. The speaker also says there is no quick fix for the social problems behind these harms.

talks.title: Privacy's Defender - How Hackers Protected the Net Before & Can Do It Again
talks.teaser: Traces how court fights over encryption export rules and NSA mass surveillance shaped online privacy, and what technologists can do next.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the case for privacy as a limit on power, from abusers using spyware against partners to insurers and governments using personal data against people. The speaker then goes back to the 1990s, when US export rules classed strong encryption software as a munition. A mathematics student's challenge, Bernstein v. Department of Justice, argued that publishing encryption code is protected speech under the First Amendment. The courts agreed, and the government eventually loosened its grip on encryption, which opened the way for the protections people use today.

The middle section covers the post-9/11 fight against NSA mass surveillance. It describes how an AT&T technician, Mark Klein, gave the Electronic Frontier Foundation evidence of backbone tapping, and how litigation, media pressure and reforms followed. The talk also covers national security letters, a gag-order fight, and recent debates over Section 702 and warrant requirements. The question round touched on border device searches, AI regulation, age verification, and surveillance of protesters and reproductive care.

The closing advice is aimed at engineers and hackers. Build encryption and privacy-preserving defaults into products, minimize data retention, and make secure tools usable for people who do not code. The speaker also urges listeners to press their representatives on warrant rules and to support digital rights organizations.
